Some [authors](/wiki/Author "Author"), such as [Tade Thompson](/wiki/Tade_Thompson "Tade Thompson") and [Jeff VanderMeer](/wiki/Jeff_VanderMeer "Jeff VanderMeer"), have observed that stories focusing explicitly on [physics](/wiki/Physics "Physics"), [astronomy](/wiki/Astronomy "Astronomy"), [mathematics](/wiki/Mathematics "Mathematics"), and [engineering](/wiki/Engineering "Engineering") tend to be considered hard science fiction, while stories focusing on [botany](/wiki/Botany "Botany"), [mycology](/wiki/Mycology "Mycology"), [zoology](/wiki/Zoology "Zoology"), and the [social sciences](/wiki/Social_science "Social science") tend to be considered soft science fiction (regardless of the relative rigor of the science).^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}229[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-tor.com-229)^

[Max Gladstone](/wiki/Max_Gladstone "Max Gladstone") defined hard science fiction as stories \"where the [math](/wiki/Mathematics "Mathematics") works\", but he pointed out that this definition identifies stories that often seem \"weirdly dated\", as scientific [paradigms](/wiki/Paradigm "Paradigm") shift over time.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}230[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-230)^ [Michael Swanwick](/wiki/Michael_Swanwick "Michael Swanwick") dismissed the traditional definition of hard science fiction altogether, instead stating that it was defined by characters striving to solve problems \"in the right way--with determination, a touch of stoicism, and the consciousness that the [universe](/wiki/Universe "Universe") is not on his or her side.\"^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}229[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-tor.com-229)^

[Ursula K. Le Guin](/wiki/Ursula_K._Le_Guin "Ursula K. Le Guin") also criticized the traditional contrast between hard and soft science fiction: \"The \'hard\' science fiction writers dismiss everything except, well, physics, astronomy, and maybe [chemistry](/wiki/Chemistry "Chemistry"). [Biology](/wiki/Biology "Biology"), [sociology](/wiki/Sociology "Sociology"), [anthropology](/wiki/Anthropology "Anthropology")---that\'s not [science](/wiki/Science "Science") to them, that\'s soft stuff. They\'re not that interested in what human beings do, really. But I am. I draw on the social sciences a great deal.\"^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}231[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-231)^

### Literary merit {#Literary_merit}

[[\[]{.mw-editsection-bracket}[edit](/w/index.php?title=Science_fiction&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Literary merit")[\]]{.mw-editsection-bracket}]{.mw-editsection}

Further information: [Literature](/wiki/Literature "Literature") and [Literary fiction](/wiki/Literary_fiction "Literary fiction")

<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb">
<a href="/wiki/File:Frontispiece_to_Frankenstein_1831.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e6/Frontispiece_to_Frankenstein_1831.jpg/250px-Frontispiece_to_Frankenstein_1831.jpg" class="mw-file-element mw-file-upright" style="--mw-file-upright: 0.75" data-file-height="3636" data-file-width="2816" decoding="async" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e6/Frontispiece_to_Frankenstein_1831.jpg/500px-Frontispiece_to_Frankenstein_1831.jpg 2x" width="190" height="245" alt="Engraving showing a naked man awaking on the floor and another man fleeing in horror. A skull and a book are next to the naked man and a window, with the moon shining through it, is in the background" /></a>
<figcaption>Illustration by <a href="/wiki/Theodor_von_Holst" title="Theodor von Holst">Theodor von Holst</a> for the 1831 edition of <a href="/wiki/Mary_Shelley" title="Mary Shelley">Mary Shelley</a>'s novel <em>Frankenstein</em><sup><a href="#cite_note-232"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>232<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup></figcaption>
</figure>

Many critics remain skeptical of the [literary value](/wiki/Literary_value "Literary value"){.mw-redirect} of science fiction and other forms of [genre fiction](/wiki/Genre_fiction "Genre fiction"), though some mainstream authors have written works claimed by opponents to be science fiction. [Mary Shelley](/wiki/Mary_Shelley "Mary Shelley") wrote a number of [scientific romance](/wiki/Scientific_romance "Scientific romance") novels in the [Gothic literature](/wiki/Gothic_literature "Gothic literature"){.mw-redirect} tradition, including *[Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus](/wiki/Frankenstein "Frankenstein")* (1818).^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}233[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-introduction-233)^ [Kurt Vonnegut](/wiki/Kurt_Vonnegut "Kurt Vonnegut") was a respected American author whose works have been argued by some to contain science fiction premises or themes.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}234[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-234)[[\[]{.cite-bracket}235[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-235)^

Other science fiction authors whose works are widely considered to be \"serious\" literature include [Ray Bradbury](/wiki/Ray_Bradbury "Ray Bradbury") (especially *[Fahrenheit 451](/wiki/Fahrenheit_451 "Fahrenheit 451")* and *[The Martian Chronicles](/wiki/The_Martian_Chronicles "The Martian Chronicles")*),^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}236[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-NYT-20120606-236)^ [Arthur C. Clarke](/wiki/Arthur_C._Clarke "Arthur C. Clarke") (especially *[Childhood\'s End](/wiki/Childhood%27s_End "Childhood's End")*),^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}237[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-237)[[\[]{.cite-bracket}238[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-238)^ and Paul Myron Anthony Linebarger (using the pseudonym [Cordwainer Smith](/wiki/Cordwainer_Smith "Cordwainer Smith")).^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}239[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-239)^ [Doris Lessing](/wiki/Doris_Lessing "Doris Lessing"), who was later awarded the [Nobel Prize in Literature](/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature "Nobel Prize in Literature"), wrote a series of five science fiction novels, *[Canopus in Argos: Archives](/wiki/Canopus_in_Argos "Canopus in Argos")* (1979--1983); these novels depict the efforts of more advanced species and civilizations to influence less advanced ones, including humans on Earth.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}240[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-Hazelton-240)[[\[]{.cite-bracket}241[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-Galin-241)[[\[]{.cite-bracket}242[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-242)[[\[]{.cite-bracket}243[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-Donoghue-243)^

[David Barnett](/wiki/David_Barnett_(writer) "David Barnett (writer)") has indicated that some novels use recognizable science fiction [tropes](/wiki/Trope_(literature) "Trope (literature)"){.mw-redirect}, but they are not classified by their authors and publishers as science fiction; such novels include *[The Road](/wiki/The_Road "The Road")* (2006) by [Cormac McCarthy](/wiki/Cormac_McCarthy "Cormac McCarthy"), *[Cloud Atlas](/wiki/Cloud_Atlas_(novel) "Cloud Atlas (novel)")* (2004) by [David Mitchell](/wiki/David_Mitchell_(author) "David Mitchell (author)"), *[The Gone-Away World](/wiki/The_Gone-Away_World "The Gone-Away World")* (2008) by [Nick Harkaway](/wiki/Nick_Harkaway "Nick Harkaway"), *[The Stone Gods](/wiki/The_Stone_Gods_(novel) "The Stone Gods (novel)")* (2007) by [Jeanette Winterson](/wiki/Jeanette_Winterson "Jeanette Winterson"), and *[Oryx and Crake](/wiki/Oryx_and_Crake "Oryx and Crake")* (2003) by [Margaret Atwood](/wiki/Margaret_Atwood "Margaret Atwood").^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}244[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-guardian4-244)^ Atwood argued against categorizing works such as *[the Handmaid\'s Tale](/wiki/The_Handmaid%27s_Tale "The Handmaid's Tale")* as science fiction; instead she labeled this novel, *Oryx and Crake*, and *[The Testaments](/wiki/The_Testaments "The Testaments")* as [speculative fiction](/wiki/Speculative_fiction "Speculative fiction").^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}245[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-Wilderness-245)^ She criticized science fiction as \"talking squids in outer space.\"^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}246[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-langford-246)^

In his book *[The Western Canon](/wiki/The_Western_Canon "The Western Canon")*, literary critic [Harold Bloom](/wiki/Harold_Bloom "Harold Bloom") includes the novels *[Brave New World](/wiki/Brave_New_World "Brave New World")*, [Stanisław Lem](/wiki/Stanis%C5%82aw_Lem "Stanisław Lem")\'s *[Solaris](/wiki/Solaris_(novel) "Solaris (novel)")*, [Kurt Vonnegut](/wiki/Kurt_Vonnegut "Kurt Vonnegut")\'s *[Cat\'s Cradle](/wiki/Cat%27s_Cradle "Cat's Cradle")*, and *[The Left Hand of Darkness](/wiki/The_Left_Hand_of_Darkness "The Left Hand of Darkness")* as culturally and aesthetically significant works of Western literature, though Lem actively spurned the label *science fiction*.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}247[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-SFWA-247)^

In her 1976 essay \"Science Fiction and Mrs Brown\", [Ursula K. Le Guin](/wiki/Ursula_K._Le_Guin "Ursula K. Le Guin") was asked, \"Can a science fiction writer write a novel?\" She answered that \"I believe that all novels \... deal with [character](/wiki/Character_(arts) "Character (arts)")\... The great novelists have brought us to see whatever they wish us to see through some character. Otherwise, they would not be novelists, but poets, historians, or pamphleteers.\"^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}248[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-harpercollins-248)^

[Orson Scott Card](/wiki/Orson_Scott_Card "Orson Scott Card") is best known for his 1985 science fiction novel *[Ender\'s Game](/wiki/Ender%27s_Game "Ender's Game")*; he has postulated that in science fiction, the message and intellectual significance of the work are contained within the story itself---therefore the genre can omit accepted literary devices and techniques that he characterized as [gimmicks](/wiki/Gimmick "Gimmick") or literary games.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}249[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-google-249)[[\[]{.cite-bracket}250[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-250)^

In 1998, [Jonathan Lethem](/wiki/Jonathan_Lethem "Jonathan Lethem") wrote an [essay](/wiki/Essay "Essay") titled \"Close Encounters: The Squandered Promise of Science Fiction\" in the *[Village Voice](/wiki/Village_Voice "Village Voice"){.mw-redirect}*. In this essay, he recalled the time in 1973 when [Thomas Pynchon](/wiki/Thomas_Pynchon "Thomas Pynchon")\'s novel *[Gravity\'s Rainbow](/wiki/Gravity%27s_Rainbow "Gravity's Rainbow")* was nominated for the [Nebula Award](/wiki/Nebula_Award "Nebula Award") and was passed over in favor of Arthur C. Clarke\'s novel *[Rendezvous with Rama](/wiki/Rendezvous_with_Rama "Rendezvous with Rama")*; Lethem suggests that this point stands as \"a hidden tombstone marking the death of the hope that SF was about to merge with the mainstream.\"^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}251[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-encounters-251)^ In the same year, science fiction author and physicist [Gregory Benford](/wiki/Gregory_Benford "Gregory Benford") wrote that \"SF is perhaps the defining genre of the twentieth century, although its conquering armies are still camped outside the [Rome](/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire") of the literary citadels.\"^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}252[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-september-252)^

## Community {#Community}

[[\[]{.mw-editsection-bracket}[edit](/w/index.php?title=Science_fiction&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Community")[\]]{.mw-editsection-bracket}]{.mw-editsection}

### Authors {#Authors}

[[\[]{.mw-editsection-bracket}[edit](/w/index.php?title=Science_fiction&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Authors")[\]]{.mw-editsection-bracket}]{.mw-editsection}

See also: [List of science fiction authors](/wiki/List_of_science_fiction_authors "List of science fiction authors"){.mw-redirect}

Science fiction has been written by authors from diverse [cultural](/wiki/Cultural_diversity "Cultural diversity") and geographical backgrounds. Among submissions to the science fiction publisher [Tor Books](/wiki/Tor_Books "Tor Books"), men account for 78% and women account for 22% (according to 2013 statistics from the publisher).^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}253[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-253)^ A [controversy](/wiki/2015_Hugo_Awards_controversy "2015 Hugo Awards controversy"){.mw-redirect} about voting slates for the 2015 [Hugo Awards](/wiki/Hugo_Award "Hugo Award") highlighted a tension in the science fiction community between two things: a trend toward increasingly diverse works and authors being honored by awards, and a reaction by groups of authors and fans who preferred more \"traditional\" science fiction.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}254[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-The_A.V._Club_6_April_2015-254)^

### Awards {#Awards}

[[\[]{.mw-editsection-bracket}[edit](/w/index.php?title=Science_fiction&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Awards")[\]]{.mw-editsection-bracket}]{.mw-editsection}

Main article: [List of science fiction awards](/wiki/List_of_science_fiction_awards "List of science fiction awards"){.mw-redirect}

Among the most significant and well-known awards for science fiction are the [Hugo Award](/wiki/Hugo_Award "Hugo Award") for [literature](/wiki/Literature "Literature"), presented by the [World Science Fiction Society](/wiki/World_Science_Fiction_Society "World Science Fiction Society"){.mw-redirect} at [Worldcon](/wiki/Worldcon "Worldcon"), and voted on by fans;^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}255[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-255)^ the [Nebula Award](/wiki/Nebula_Award "Nebula Award") for literature, presented by the [Science Fiction and Fantasy Writers of America](/wiki/Science_Fiction_and_Fantasy_Writers_of_America "Science Fiction and Fantasy Writers of America"){.mw-redirect}, and voted on by the community of authors;^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}256[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-256)^ the [John W. Campbell Memorial Award for Best Science Fiction Novel](/wiki/John_W._Campbell_Memorial_Award_for_Best_Science_Fiction_Novel "John W. Campbell Memorial Award for Best Science Fiction Novel"), presented by a jury of writers;^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}257[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-257)^ and the [Theodore Sturgeon Memorial Award](/wiki/Theodore_Sturgeon_Award "Theodore Sturgeon Award") for [short fiction](/wiki/Short_story "Short story"), presented by a jury.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}258[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-258)^ One notable award for science fiction films and TV programs is the [Saturn Award](/wiki/Saturn_Award "Saturn Award"){.mw-redirect}, which is presented annually by [The Academy of Science Fiction, Fantasy, and Horror Films](/wiki/Academy_of_Science_Fiction,_Fantasy_and_Horror_Films "Academy of Science Fiction, Fantasy and Horror Films").^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}259[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-259)^

There are other national awards, like Canada\'s [Prix Aurora Awards](/wiki/Prix_Aurora_Awards "Prix Aurora Awards"){.mw-redirect},^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}260[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-260)^ regional awards, like the [Endeavour Award](/wiki/Endeavour_Award "Endeavour Award") presented at [Orycon](/wiki/OryCon "OryCon"){.mw-redirect} for works from the [U.S. Pacific Northwest](/wiki/Pacific_Northwest "Pacific Northwest"),^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}261[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-261)^ and special interest or [subgenre](/wiki/Subgenre "Subgenre"){.mw-redirect} awards such as the [Chesley Award](/wiki/Chesley_Award "Chesley Award"){.mw-redirect} for art, presented by the Association of Science Fiction & Fantasy Artists,^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}262[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-262)^ or the [World Fantasy Award](/wiki/World_Fantasy_Award "World Fantasy Award") for fantasy.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}263[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-263)^ Magazines may organize reader polls, notably the [Locus Award](/wiki/Locus_Award "Locus Award").^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}264[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-264)^

### Conventions {#Conventions}

[[\[]{.mw-editsection-bracket}[edit](/w/index.php?title=Science_fiction&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Conventions")[\]]{.mw-editsection-bracket}]{.mw-editsection}

Main article: [Science fiction convention](/wiki/Science_fiction_convention "Science fiction convention")

<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb">
<a href="/wiki/File:Sfcon-reading-ddb.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/25/Sfcon-reading-ddb.jpg/250px-Sfcon-reading-ddb.jpg" class="mw-file-element" data-file-height="391" data-file-width="700" decoding="async" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/25/Sfcon-reading-ddb.jpg/500px-Sfcon-reading-ddb.jpg 2x" width="250" height="140" /></a>
<figcaption>Writer <a href="/wiki/Pamela_Dean" title="Pamela Dean">Pamela Dean</a> reading at the Minneapolis convention known as <a href="/wiki/Minicon" title="Minicon">Minicon</a> in 2006</figcaption>
</figure>

[Conventions](/wiki/Convention_(meeting) "Convention (meeting)") (often abbreviated by fans as *cons*, such as [Comic-con](/wiki/Comic-con "Comic-con"){.mw-redirect}) are held in cities around the world; these cater to a local, regional, national, or international membership.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}265[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-265)[[\[]{.cite-bracket}53[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-Encyclopedia_Britannica-53)[[\[]{.cite-bracket}266[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-266)^ General-interest conventions cover all aspects of science fiction, while others focus on a particular interest such as [media fandom](/wiki/Media_fandom "Media fandom"){.mw-redirect} or [filk music](/wiki/Filking "Filking"){.mw-redirect}.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}267[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-267)[[\[]{.cite-bracket}268[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-268)^ Most science fiction conventions are organized by volunteers in non-profit groups, though most media-oriented events are organized by commercial promoters.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}269[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-269)^

### Fandom and fanzines {#Fandom_and_fanzines}

[[\[]{.mw-editsection-bracket}[edit](/w/index.php?title=Science_fiction&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Fandom and fanzines")[\]]{.mw-editsection-bracket}]{.mw-editsection}

Main articles: [Science fiction fandom](/wiki/Science_fiction_fandom "Science fiction fandom") and [Science-fiction fanzine](/wiki/Science-fiction_fanzine "Science-fiction fanzine")

<figure class="mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb">
<a href="/wiki/File:MGNTNJNRNL1938.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f9/MGNTNJNRNL1938.jpg/250px-MGNTNJNRNL1938.jpg" class="mw-file-element" data-file-height="600" data-file-width="419" decoding="async" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f9/MGNTNJNRNL1938.jpg 2x" width="200" height="286" /></a>
<figcaption>Cover of <em>Imagination</em>, a fanzine published by Forrest J. Ackerman, January 1938, drawn by Jim Mooney</figcaption>
</figure>

Science fiction [fandom](/wiki/Science_fiction_fandom "Science fiction fandom") emerged from the letters column in *[Amazing Stories](/wiki/Amazing_Stories "Amazing Stories")* magazine. Fans began writing letters to each other, and then assembling their comments in informal publications that became known as [*fanzines*](/wiki/Fanzine "Fanzine").^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}270[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-fanzine_history-270)^ Once in regular communication, these fans wanted to meet in person, so they organized local clubs.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}270[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-fanzine_history-270)[[\[]{.cite-bracket}271[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-fancyclopedia_con-271)^ During the 1930s, the first science fiction [conventions](/wiki/Science_fiction_conventions "Science fiction conventions"){.mw-redirect} gathered fans from a larger area.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}271[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-fancyclopedia_con-271)^

The earliest organized online fandom was the SF Lovers Community, originally a [mailing list](/wiki/Mailing_list "Mailing list") in the late 1970s, with a text [archive file](/wiki/File_archiver "File archiver") that was updated regularly.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}272[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-sf-lovers_hist-272)^ In the 1980s, [Usenet](/wiki/Usenet "Usenet") groups greatly expanded the circle of fans [online](/wiki/Online_and_offline "Online and offline").^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}273[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-273)^ In the 1990s, the development of the [World-Wide Web](/wiki/World-Wide_Web "World-Wide Web"){.mw-redirect} increased online fandom through [websites](/wiki/Website "Website") devoted to science fiction and related [genres](/wiki/Genre "Genre") in all media.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}274[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-fan_clubhouse-274)\[*[[failed\ verification]{title="The material near this tag failed verification of its source citation(s). (January 2025)"}](/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")*\]^

The first science fiction fanzine, *[The Comet](/wiki/The_Comet_(fanzine) "The Comet (fanzine)")*, was published in 1930 by the Science Correspondence Club in Chicago, Illinois.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}275[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-first_fanzine-275)[[\[]{.cite-bracket}276[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-276)^ As of 2025, one of the best known fanzines is *[Ansible](/wiki/Ansible_(magazine) "Ansible (magazine)"){.mw-redirect}*, edited by [David Langford](/wiki/David_Langford "David Langford"), winner of numerous [Hugo awards](/wiki/Hugo_Award "Hugo Award").^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}277[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-277)[[\[]{.cite-bracket}278[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-278)^ Other notable fanzines to win one or more Hugo awards include *[File 770](/wiki/File_770 "File 770")*, *[Mimosa](/wiki/Mimosa_(magazine) "Mimosa (magazine)")*, and *[Plokta](/wiki/Plokta "Plokta")*.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}279[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-The_Hugo_Awards-2007-279)^ Artists working for fanzines have often risen to prominence in the field, including [Brad W. Foster](/wiki/Brad_W._Foster "Brad W. Foster"), [Teddy Harvia](/wiki/Teddy_Harvia "Teddy Harvia"), and Joe Mayhew; the Hugo Awards include a category for [Best Fan Artists](/wiki/Hugo_Award_for_Best_Fan_Artist "Hugo Award for Best Fan Artist").^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}279[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-The_Hugo_Awards-2007-279)^

## Elements {#Elements}

[[\[]{.mw-editsection-bracket}[edit](/w/index.php?title=Science_fiction&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Elements")[\]]{.mw-editsection-bracket}]{.mw-editsection}

<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb">
<a href="/wiki/File:Future_Birthplace_of_Captain_James_T_Kirk.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/Future_Birthplace_of_Captain_James_T_Kirk.jpg/250px-Future_Birthplace_of_Captain_James_T_Kirk.jpg" class="mw-file-element" data-file-height="879" data-file-width="1194" decoding="async" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/Future_Birthplace_of_Captain_James_T_Kirk.jpg/500px-Future_Birthplace_of_Captain_James_T_Kirk.jpg 2x" width="250" height="184" /></a>
<figcaption>Plaque in <a href="/wiki/Riverside,_Iowa" title="Riverside, Iowa">Riverside, Iowa</a>, to honor the "future birth" of <em><a href="/wiki/Star_Trek" title="Star Trek">Star Trek</a></em><span class="nowrap" style="padding-left:0.1em;">'</span>s character <a href="/wiki/James_T._Kirk" title="James T. Kirk">James T. Kirk</a></figcaption>
</figure>

Science fiction elements can include the following:

-   Temporal settings in the future or in [alternative histories](/wiki/Alternative_histories "Alternative histories"){.mw-redirect};^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}280[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-counterfact-280)^
-   Predicted or speculative technology such as [brain-computer interface](/wiki/Brain-computer_interface "Brain-computer interface"){.mw-redirect}, [bio-engineering](/wiki/Bio-engineering "Bio-engineering"){.mw-redirect}, [superintelligent](/wiki/Superintelligent "Superintelligent"){.mw-redirect} [computers](/wiki/Computer "Computer"), [robots](/wiki/Robot "Robot"), [ray guns](/wiki/Ray_guns "Ray guns"){.mw-redirect}, and [advanced weapons](/wiki/Weapons_in_science_fiction "Weapons in science fiction");^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}281[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-GW-281)[[\[]{.cite-bracket}282[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-How_to_Write_Science_Fiction_and_Fantasy-282)^
-   [Space travel](/wiki/Space_travel_in_science_fiction "Space travel in science fiction"), or settings in [outer space](/wiki/Outer_space "Outer space"), on other worlds, in [subterranean earth](/wiki/Hollow_Earth "Hollow Earth"),^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}283[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-DK-2015-283)^ or in [parallel universes](/wiki/Parallel_universe_(fiction)#Science_fiction "Parallel universe (fiction)"){.mw-redirect};^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}284[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-britannica-284)^
-   [Fictional concepts in biology](/wiki/Biology_in_fiction "Biology in fiction") such as [aliens](/wiki/Extraterrestrial_life "Extraterrestrial life"), [mutants](/wiki/Mutants_in_fiction "Mutants in fiction"), and [enhanced humans](/wiki/Enhanced_human "Enhanced human"){.mw-redirect};^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}281[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-GW-281)[[\[]{.cite-bracket}285[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-Parker-285)^
-   Undiscovered scientific possibilities such as [teleportation](/wiki/Teleportation "Teleportation"), [time travel](/wiki/Time_travel "Time travel"), and [faster-than-light](/wiki/Faster-than-light "Faster-than-light") travel or [communication](/wiki/Ansible "Ansible");^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}286[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-286)^
-   Social/political systems and situations that are new and different, including [utopian](/wiki/Utopian "Utopian"){.mw-redirect},^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}283[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-DK-2015-283)^ [dystopian](/wiki/Dystopia "Dystopia"), [post-apocalyptic](/wiki/Post-apocalyptic "Post-apocalyptic"){.mw-redirect}, or [post-scarcity](/wiki/Post-scarcity "Post-scarcity");^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}287[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-287)^
-   [Future history](/wiki/Future_history "Future history") and [speculative evolution](/wiki/Speculative_evolution "Speculative evolution") of humans on Earth or other planets;^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}288[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-Ashley-288)^
-   [Paranormal](/wiki/Paranormal "Paranormal") abilities such as [mind control](/wiki/Mind_control_in_popular_culture "Mind control in popular culture"), [telepathy](/wiki/Telepathy "Telepathy"), and [telekinesis](/wiki/Telekinesis "Telekinesis").^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}289[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-289)^
-   [Religious fanaticism](/wiki/Religious_fanaticism "Religious fanaticism") is heavily intertwined with science fiction through its use of [ritual](/wiki/Ritual "Ritual") and [extremism](/wiki/Extremism "Extremism") to interpret or misinterpret the world.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}290[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-290)^ The science fiction questions cultural norms, trends, and social movements. [Religion](/wiki/Religion "Religion") and religious fanaticism critique the world in the same way as science fiction, while the stories display a disconnect between the extreme actions of a fanatic and the typical protagonist, who often combats this element.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}291[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-291)^

<figure class="mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb">
<a href="/wiki/File:Climate_fiction_-_Outdoor_agriculture_in_India_in_2500.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1c/Climate_fiction_-_Outdoor_agriculture_in_India_in_2500.jpg/330px-Climate_fiction_-_Outdoor_agriculture_in_India_in_2500.jpg" class="mw-file-element" data-file-height="425" data-file-width="1032" decoding="async" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1c/Climate_fiction_-_Outdoor_agriculture_in_India_in_2500.jpg/960px-Climate_fiction_-_Outdoor_agriculture_in_India_in_2500.jpg 2x" width="300" height="124" /></a>
<figcaption>A <a href="/wiki/Climate_fiction" title="Climate fiction">climate fiction</a> depiction of agriculture in India in 2500, with workers wearing protective suits to protect from extreme temperatures and <a href="/wiki/Unmanned_surface_vehicle" title="Unmanned surface vehicle">unmanned surface vehicle</a> tractors.</figcaption>
</figure>

While science fiction is a genre of fiction, a science fiction genre is a subgenre within science fiction. Science fiction may be divided along any number of overlapping axes. Gary K. Wolfe\'s *Critical Terms for Science Fiction and Fantasy* identifies over 30 subdivisions of science fiction, not including [science fantasy](/wiki/Science_fantasy "Science fantasy") (which is a [mixed genre](/wiki/Mixed_genre "Mixed genre"){.mw-redirect}).

[\"21st Century Brands\"](http://www.cbc.ca/undertheinfluence/season-3/2014/05/24/21st-century-brands-1/){.external .text rel="nofollow"}. [*Under the Influence*](/wiki/Under_the_Influence_(radio_documentary_series) "Under the Influence (radio documentary series)"){.mw-redirect}. Season 3. Episode 21. Event occurs at time 2:07. CBC Radio One. [Archived](https://web.archive.org/web/20140608190711/http://www.cbc.ca/undertheinfluence/season-3/2014/05/24/21st-century-brands-1/){.external .text rel="nofollow"} from the original on 8 June 2014. [Transcript of the original source](http://www.cbc.ca/undertheinfluence/season-3/2014/05/24/21st-century-brands-1/){.external .text rel="nofollow"}[. Retrieved [7 June]{.nowrap} 2014]{.reference-accessdate}. "The series had lots of interesting devices that marveled us back in the 1960s. In episode one, we see wife Jane doing exercises in front of a flatscreen television. In another episode, we see George Jetson reading the newspaper on a screen. Can anyone say tablet? In another, Boss Spacely tells George to fix something called a \"computer virus\". Everyone on the show uses video chat, foreshadowing Skype and Face Time. There is a robot vacuum cleaner, foretelling the 2002 arrival of the iRobot Roomba vacuum. There was also a tanning bed used in an episode, a product that wasn\'t introduced to North America until 1979. And while flying space cars that have yet to land in our lives, the Jetsons show had moving sidewalks like we now have in airports, treadmills that didn\'t hit the consumer market until 1969, and they had a repairman who had a piece of technology called\... Mac."[]{.Z3988 title="ctx_ver=Z39.88-2004&rft_val_fmt=info%3Aofi%2Ffmt%3Akev%3Amtx%3Abook&rft.genre=unknown&rft.btitle=Under+the+Influence&rft.series=Season+3.+Episode+21&rft.date=2014-05-24&rft.aulast=O%27Reilly&rft.aufirst=Terry&rft_id=http%3A%2F%2Fwww.cbc.ca%2Fundertheinfluence%2Fseason-3%2F2014%2F05%2F24%2F21st-century-brands-1%2F&rfr_id=info%3Asid%2Fen.wikipedia.org%3AScience+fiction"}]{.reference-text}]{#cite_note-152}
